title: k-means clustering, and what comes next
summary: Find groups with no labels, then map everything you built to scikit-learn.

steps.title: k-means
body: **k-means** splits unlabelled points into `k` groups. Start with `k` centres, then repeat:
1. **assign** every point to its nearest centre;
2. **update** each centre to the mean of the points assigned to it;

until the assignments stop changing. It is used for customer segments, colour compression and as a quick look at structure. You choose `k`, and the result depends on the starting centres, so libraries try several starts.
The distance from every point to every centre is one broadcast:
```python
d = np.sqrt(((X[:, None, :] - centres[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(axis=2))   # shape (n, k)
labels = d.argmin(axis=1)

lines: centres = np.array([X[labels == j].mean(axis=0) for j in range(k)])

steps.explain: One row per point, one column per centre. (5, 6) is a little closer to (10, 10): squared distance 41 versus 61.

steps.title: Assign and update
prompt: Write the two halves of k-means:
- `assign(X, centres)`: an array of the index of the nearest centre for each row of `X` (broadcasting, no loops).
- `update(X, labels, k)`: a `(k, features)` array whose row `j` is the mean of the points labelled `j`.
solution: return np.array([X[labels == j].mean(axis=0) for j in range(k)])
hints: `X[:, None, :] - centres[None, :, :]` has shape (n, k, features).
`X[labels == j].mean(axis=0)` is the new centre j.

steps.title: k-means from start to finish
prompt: Write `kmeans(X, init, iters=50)` that starts from the centres `init` (a `(k, features)` array) and alternates assign and update until the labels stop changing (or `iters` rounds). Return `(labels, centres)`.
Then write `inertia(X, labels, centres)`: the total squared distance from each point to its own centre, a plain float rounded to 2. Lower is tighter.
solution: if labels is not None and (new == labels).all():
centres = np.array([X[labels == j].mean(axis=0) for j in range(k)])
hints: Keep the previous labels and `break` when `(new == labels).all()`.
For inertia, `centres[labels]` gives each point's own centre.

Dojo.check("centres land near the true centres", all(_np.min(_np.linalg.norm(_c - t, axis=1)) < 0.4 for t in _true), str(_np.round(_c, 2).tolist()))

steps.title: Next steps: scikit-learn
body: You now know what the standard tools do inside. In real projects reach for **scikit-learn** (`pip install scikit-learn`): every model has the same `fit` / `predict` API, tested and fast.
```python
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)
model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5))
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)                       # scaler learns train mean/std only: no leakage
model.score(X_te, y_te)                     # accuracy
cross_val_score(model, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5)    # 5 train/validate splits, to choose k honestly

A **pipeline** bundles preprocessing with the model so the scaling is always fitted on training data. **Cross-validation** rotates which slice is held out, so you can tune settings without touching the test set. Other models you will meet: `LinearRegression`, `LogisticRegression`, `RandomForestClassifier`, `KMeans`, and `sklearn.metrics` for `mean_absolute_error`, `precision_score`, `confusion_matrix`.

steps.prompt: Why use cross-validation to choose `k` for kNN instead of the test set?
options: Tuning on the test set makes it part of training, so its score is no longer an honest estimate
Cross-validation makes the model more accurate on its own
The test set is too small to compute accuracy
scikit-learn does not allow scoring on a test set

steps.title: Your own fit/predict API
prompt: Package your kNN in a class with the scikit-learn shape, so it could be swapped for the real thing:
model = KNNClassifier(k=3).fit(X_train, y_train)   # fit returns self
model.score(X_test, y_test)  # accuracy, plain float rounded to 3
`fit` should **standardise** using the training mean and std (store them on `self`), and `predict` must apply the same scaling to new data before measuring distances.
hints: In `fit`, store `self.mu`, `self.sd` and the scaled training data, then `return self`.
In `predict`, scale X with the stored `mu` and `sd`, then run your kNN vote per row.
